main.title: Golden Joystick Awards 1992
main.summary: The Golden Joystick Awards, with every category winner of the 1992/1993 edition.

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.

main.title: Streets of Rage 2
main.subtitle: Four fighters against Mr. X
main.summary: Streets of Rage 2, known as Bare Knuckle II in Japan, is a 1992 beat 'em up video game developed by Ancient and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis.

cards.heading: Axel and Blaze return with two new fighters
cards.text:
Streets of Rage 2, known as Bare Knuckle II in Japan, is a 1992 beat 'em up video game developed by Ancient and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis. The sequel to Streets of Rage (1991), the characters Axel Stone and Blaze Fielding return while the game also introduces two new characters: Max Thunder, and Eddie "Skate" Hunter, the younger brother of Adam Hunter from the first game.

Streets of Rage 2 was developed by an ad hoc team of several companies: Ancient, Shout! Design Works, M.N.M Software, and H.I.C. Ancient's Ayano Koshiro was the lead graphic designer and one of the game design planners, while her brother Yuzo Koshiro composed the music.

cards.heading: Blitz attacks, special moves and two-player combat
cards.text: Like the previous game, Streets of Rage 2 is a side-scrolling beat-em-up in which one or two players fight against waves of enemies while picking up weapons and items along the way. Along with returning characters Axel Stone and Blaze Fielding, the game introduces two new characters; Max Thunder, a slow-moving but powerful wrestler, and Eddie "Skate" Hunter (known as Sammy Hunter in the Japanese release), the brother of previous game's Adam Hunter who can move around quickly with his rollerblades. In addition to standard attacks, which have been expanded from the previous game, each character can perform a unique Blitz Attack by double tapping a direction before attacking. Replacing the police car attack from the previous game, each character can perform Special Attacks which can deal extra damage or attack enemies from all directions at the cost of the player's health. Along with the main campaign, two players can also fight against each other in the game's Duel mode.

cards.heading: Ayano Koshiro designs the fighters and combat
cards.text: Ancient's Ayano Koshiro served as the lead graphic designer and one of the planners on the game design team. She designed the graphics, characters, and combat mechanics. Her brother Yuzo Koshiro, the lead music composer, also provided some input on the combat. The brother-sister team took inspiration from Capcom's Street Fighter II, an arcade cabinet of which they had installed at the Ancient office. The hit arcade video game influenced the combat system of Streets of Rage 2.

cards.heading: A dance soundtrack built on the PC-8801
cards.text:
The soundtrack for Streets of Rage 2 was composed by Yuzo Koshiro, along with three contributions from Motohiro Kawashima. It was composed using then outdated NEC PC-8801 hardware alongside Koshiro's own audio programming language. According to Koshiro: "For Bare Knuckle I used the PC88 and an original programming language I developed myself. The original was called MML, Music Macro Language. It's based on NEC's BASIC program, but I modified it heavily. It was more a BASIC-style language at first, but I modified it to be something more like Assembly. I called it Music Love'. I used it for all the Bare Knuckle Games."

The soundtrack was influenced by electronic dance music, specifically house, techno, hardcore techno, and breakbeat. The soundtrack for Streets of Rage 2 is considered "revolutionary" and ahead of its time, for its "blend of swaggering house synths", "dirty" electro-funk and "trancey electronic textures that would feel as comfortable in a nightclub as a video game."

main.title: Taz-Mania
main.subtitle: An appetite for adventure
main.summary: Taz-Mania, developed by Recreational Brainware and published by Sega in 1992, turns the Tasmanian Devil’s appetite into the motive for a Mega Drive adventure. A story about a gigantic seabird egg sends Taz across Tasmania in search of an extraordinary meal. This 16-bit game is a separate design from the Game Gear, Master System and Super Nintendo titles that share the license.

cards.heading: An appetite for adventure
cards.text: Taz-Mania, developed by Recreational Brainware and published by Sega in 1992, turns the Tasmanian Devil’s appetite into the motive for a Mega Drive adventure. A story about a gigantic seabird egg sends Taz across Tasmania in search of an extraordinary meal. This 16-bit game is a separate design from the Game Gear, Master System and Super Nintendo titles that share the license.

cards.heading: Spinning, grabbing and eating
cards.text: His characteristic whirlwind becomes an attack that breaks through enemies and obstacles. Taz can also pick up objects and eat food to recover energy; chili peppers add a breath of fire. Hunger is therefore part of the action, while careless handling of dangerous objects can work against him. The comedy comes from what Taz does as much as from how he looks.

cards.heading: A cartoon built around movement
cards.text: Desert landscapes give way to factories, ice and mines, including a runaway mine-cart sequence. Oversized gestures and abrupt changes in expression carry the cartoon into the movement of a sprite. Rather than asking the player to control a whole animated cast, the game builds its routes and hazards around one character’s spinning, grabbing and devouring.

main.title: Dune II
main.summary: Dune II: The Building of a Dynasty (titled Dune II: Battle for Arrakis in Europe and Dune: The Battle for Arrakis in North America for the Mega Drive/Genesis port, respectively) is a 1992 real-time strategy game developed by Westwood Studios and published by Virgin Games.

cards.heading: Three houses fight for Arrakis
cards.text: Dune II: The Building of a Dynasty (titled Dune II: Battle for Arrakis in Europe and Dune: The Battle for Arrakis in North America for the Mega Drive/Genesis port, respectively) is a 1992 real-time strategy game developed by Westwood Studios and published by Virgin Games. It serves as the sequel to Dune (a more traditional adventure game), which came out earlier that same year.

cards.heading: A model for real-time strategy
cards.text: While not the first real-time strategy (RTS) video game, Dune II established the format that would be followed for years to come. As such, Dune II is the archetypal real-time strategy game. Striking a balance between complexity and innovation, it was a huge success and laid the foundation for Age of Empires, Warcraft, Westwood Studios' subsequent strategy game Command & Conquer, and many other RTS games that followed.

main.title: Alone in the Dark
main.summary: Alone in the Dark is a 1992 survival horror video game designed by Frédérick Raynal.

cards.heading: A haunted mansion in three dimensions
cards.text: Alone in the Dark is a 1992 survival horror video game designed by Frédérick Raynal. Developed and published by Infogrames in 1992 for MS-DOS, the game was eventually ported to Mac OS, the PC-98, the FM Towns, the 3DO, RISC OS, and iOS. Alone in the Dark is set in 1920s Louisiana and challenges the player to escape a haunted mansion. To advance, the player must solve puzzles while banishing, slaying, or eluding various ghosts and monsters. The player can collect and use weapons, manage a weight-based inventory system, and explore a partially nonlinear map.

cards.heading: Fixed cameras, moving characters
cards.text: Raynal was motivated to create Alone in the Dark due to his interest in 3D animation and his fondness for horror films. The storyline was inspired by the Cthulhu Mythos of H. P. Lovecraft and the work of directors like Dario Argento and George A. Romero. Raynal's programming team worked to convey much of this story via key texts scattered about the game's environment. To overcome technical limitations, the production team also employed a fixed camera angle system to dramatically frame the movement of three-dimensional characters on top of two-dimensional background images.

cards.heading: The survival horror legacy
cards.text: Upon its release, Alone in the Dark received acclaim, with critics applauding its unsettling atmosphere, effective soundtrack, and technical inventiveness. The game also won several industry awards and is regularly included in lists of the best video games ever made. Often identified as the first 3D survival horror game, Alone in the Dark strongly influenced the production of Capcom's Resident Evil (1996), and it also spawned a series of follow-up games and two films. A reimagining of the original game, published by THQ Nordic, was released on 20 March 2024.

main.title: Ecco the Dolphin
main.summary: Ecco the Dolphin is an action-adventure game developed by Ed Annunziata and Novotrade International and published by Sega for the Mega Drive/Genesis in 1992.

cards.heading: An ocean journey through time
cards.text: Ecco the Dolphin is an action-adventure game developed by Ed Annunziata and Novotrade International and published by Sega for the Mega Drive/Genesis in 1992. Versions for the Sega CD, Master System, and Game Gear were released the following years. It is the first installment in the Ecco the Dolphin video game franchise. The player character is a bottlenose dolphin who travels through time to combat hostile extraterrestrials in Earth's oceans and on an alien spacecraft.

cards.heading: A dolphin beyond the Mega Drive
cards.text: Ecco the Dolphin received favourable reviews and became a bestseller on the Genesis. It has been re-released several times, including on the Nintendo Virtual Console, Xbox Live Arcade, Steam, iOS, Nintendo 3DS, and the Nintendo Classics service. A sequel, Ecco: The Tides of Time, was released in 1994.

main.title: Wolfenstein 3D
main.summary: Wolfenstein 3D is a 1992 first-person shooter game developed by id Software and published by Apogee Software and FormGen for MS-DOS.

cards.heading: Escaping Castle Wolfenstein
cards.text: Wolfenstein 3D is a 1992 first-person shooter game developed by id Software and published by Apogee Software and FormGen for MS-DOS. It was inspired by the 1981 Muse Software video game Castle Wolfenstein, and is the third installment in the Wolfenstein series. In Wolfenstein 3D, the player assumes the role of Allied spy William "B.J." Blazkowicz during World War II as he escapes from the Nazi German prison Castle Wolfenstein and carries out a series of crucial missions against the Nazis. The player traverses each of the game's levels to find an elevator to the next level or kill a final boss, fighting Nazi soldiers, dogs, and other enemies with a knife and a variety of guns.

cards.heading: From an engine experiment to shareware
cards.text: John Carmack's experiments in Hovertank 3D and Catacomb 3-D showed how restricting movement and viewpoint could make a three-dimensional world run quickly. John Romero proposed turning Castle Wolfenstein into a faster action game, and he and Tom Hall designed around that pace. Adrian Carmack supplied the art and Bobby Prince the music and effects. Apogee released the first episode free under the shareware model, inviting players to buy the remaining episodes. Spear of Destiny then carried the same approach into a standalone retail release.

main.title: World of Illusion Starring Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck
main.subtitle: A magic act becomes an adventure
main.summary: World of Illusion Starring Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck is Sega’s 1992 Mega Drive/Genesis platform game, with its Japanese release documented on December 18.

cards.heading: A magic act becomes an adventure
cards.text: World of Illusion Starring Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck is Sega’s 1992 Mega Drive/Genesis platform game, with its Japanese release documented on December 18. While preparing a magic act, Mickey and Donald discover a mysterious box and enter a world controlled by a hostile magician. Their journey home passes through oversized landscapes, an underwater realm and a library where ordinary objects become platforms. Magical attacks take the place of conventional weapons, fitting the theatrical setting. Sega’s original artwork and animation turn the two familiar cartoon characters into stage partners caught inside a trick that has become real.

cards.heading: Two heroes, one way home
cards.text: The choice of character changes more than the portrait on screen. Mickey and Donald can be played separately, while two players can travel together and help one another through obstacles. One can give the other a lift or lower a rope, making cooperation part of movement rather than merely doubling the number of heroes. The game includes routes shaped around these different arrangements, so playing together is its own variation of the adventure. Its fantasy comes from that relationship as much as from the scenery: getting home requires both a magician’s tricks and a partner’s assistance. The original sound-team credits identify Haruyo Oguro and Tomoko Sasaki.

main.title: Bucky O’Hare
main.subtitle: Bring the crew home
main.summary: Bucky O’Hare is Konami’s NES platform action game based on the comic-book space hero. The rabbit captain’s crew has been captured and scattered across four planets, leaving Bucky to begin the rescue alone. Those first destinations can be approached in different orders. Each rescued companion then becomes playable, bringing another weapon or ability to the team. The result turns the rescue story into a changing set of controls: progress adds people whose skills can alter how the next obstacle is crossed.

cards.heading: Bring the crew home
cards.text: Bucky O’Hare is Konami’s NES platform action game based on the comic-book space hero. The rabbit captain’s crew has been captured and scattered across four planets, leaving Bucky to begin the rescue alone. Those first destinations can be approached in different orders. Each rescued companion then becomes playable, bringing another weapon or ability to the team. The result turns the rescue story into a changing set of controls: progress adds people whose skills can alter how the next obstacle is crossed.

cards.heading: A planet for each problem
cards.text: The opening worlds give the journey distinct physical challenges. The Green Planet combines trees and waterfalls, the Red Planet is dominated by volcanic heat, the Blue Planet is icy, and the Yellow Planet contains cannons and moving asteroids. Those settings ask for careful movement as well as shooting. The player can switch between available characters during play, so rescuing a companion expands the answers available to a difficult section. The order of rescue becomes a way of shaping which abilities arrive first.

cards.heading: A rescue that keeps changing hands
cards.text: Once the initial crew is reunited, the adventure moves into another captivity aboard the Magma Tanker. The company must continue saving one another and work toward escape, giving the second part a different structure from the opening choice of planets. The game combines colourful character animation with short, demanding platform sections, encouraging repeated attempts at a particular movement. Its team structure supplies continuity through those changes: the characters are both the reason for the journey and the tools with which the player completes it.

main.title: Soul Blazer
main.subtitle: Quintet · Super Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Soul Blazer is Quintet's Super Nintendo action role-playing adventure about restoring a world whose living souls have been imprisoned. The player controls a warrior sent by the Master to defeat monsters and release the people, animals and plants held inside their lairs. Settlements begin empty and gradually return to life as the surrounding dungeons are cleared. The reward for fighting is therefore visible outside the battlefield: another resident appears, a building returns or a familiar place acquires somebody who can explain what should happen next.

cards.heading: Bring the inhabitants back
cards.text: Soul Blazer is Quintet's Super Nintendo action role-playing adventure about restoring a world whose living souls have been imprisoned. The player controls a warrior sent by the Master to defeat monsters and release the people, animals and plants held inside their lairs. Settlements begin empty and gradually return to life as the surrounding dungeons are cleared. The reward for fighting is therefore visible outside the battlefield: another resident appears, a building returns or a familiar place acquires somebody who can explain what should happen next.

cards.heading: A cleared lair changes the settlement
cards.text: Destroying a monster lair releases a particular soul and reconnects it with the place it belongs. Returning to town reveals the result, and the restored inhabitant may provide advice or an item needed elsewhere. The player moves repeatedly between the dangerous area and its recovering community. Each side gives the other a purpose. A corridor leads toward the next person to rescue, while a conversation back home explains why another part of the dungeon has become important or how it can finally be crossed.

cards.heading: A world populated beyond its people
cards.text: The warrior can communicate with many kinds of living things, making a dolphin or a flower part of the adventure's social world. That broad idea of restoration gives the changing settlements their character. Sword fighting, equipment and magical assistance support the immediate action, while Yukihide Takekawa's music accompanies the different regions. Released by Enix in 1992, Soul Blazer developed Quintet's interest in making the recovery of a place playable. Its central satisfaction comes from returning somewhere that was empty and finding life waiting there because of the last journey.
